sections.title: Sounds, spelling and stress
sections.summary: Spanish spelling is almost perfectly regular: once you know a handful of letter sounds and two stress rules, you can pronounce any word you read and know when it needs a written accent.

rules.title: Five pure vowels
rules.body: Spanish has only five vowel sounds, a, e, i, o, u, and each is always pronounced the same way: short and clear, never reduced to the English 'uh' sound. 'a' is like the a in father, 'e' like the e in bet, 'i' like ee in see, 'o' like o in or, 'u' like oo in food. Two vowels side by side are each pronounced.

rules.title: ñ, ll, rr, h and j
rules.body: ñ is the sound ny in canyon: año (year), niño (child). ll is pronounced like English y in yes in most of the Spanish-speaking world: llamar, calle. rr (and r at the start of a word) is a rolled, trilled r: perro, rojo; a single r between vowels is a quick tap: pero. h is always silent: hola, hablar. j is a strong, breathy h from the back of the throat: jamón, Juan.

rules.title: c, z, g, gu and qu
rules.body: c before e or i, and z everywhere, sound like th in think in most of Spain and like s in Latin America: cena, cine, zapato. c before a, o, u is a hard k: casa, coche. qu (only before e and i) is also k, and the u is silent: queso, quince. g before e or i sounds like j (a strong h): gente, gimnasio. To keep a hard g before e or i, Spanish writes gu with a silent u: guerra, guitarra. Elsewhere g is a hard g: gato.

rules.title: b and v are the same sound
rules.body: Spanish makes no difference in sound between b and v: both are pronounced like a soft b. 'vaca' (cow) and 'baca' (roof rack) sound identical. Only spelling tells them apart, so you simply have to learn which words use which letter.

rules.title: Stress rule 1: words ending in a vowel, n or s
rules.body: If a word ends in a vowel, n or s, the stress falls naturally on the second-to-last syllable and no accent mark is written: CA-sa, ha-BLAN, LU-nes, es-tu-DIAN-te. Most Spanish words follow this pattern, so when in doubt, stress the next-to-last syllable.

rules.title: Stress rule 2: words ending in other consonants
rules.body: If a word ends in any consonant other than n or s, the stress falls naturally on the last syllable: ha-BLAR, ciu-DAD, es-pa-ÑOL, re-LOJ. All infinitives (-ar, -er, -ir) therefore stress the ending.

rules.title: The written accent marks exceptions
rules.body: When a word breaks rule 1 or rule 2, the stressed vowel carries a written accent (tilde): ca-FÉ ends in a vowel but is stressed on the last syllable; ÁR-bol ends in l but is stressed on the first. Words stressed on the third-from-last syllable always carry an accent: MÉ-di-co, SÁ-ba-do, te-LÉ-fo-no. The accent can appear or disappear in the plural: examen / exámenes, joven / jóvenes, canción / canciones.

rules.title: Accents that distinguish words
rules.body: A few one-syllable words carry an accent only to tell them apart from a look-alike: sí (yes) / si (if), él (he) / el (the), tú (you) / tu (your), mí (me) / mi (my), té (tea) / te (you, object), sé (I know) / se (reflexive). Question and exclamation words always have an accent: qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cómo, cuánto, por qué.

examples.en: I don't know if I'll have tea.

rules.title: ¿ ¡ and capital letters
rules.body: Questions and exclamations open with an upside-down mark and close with the normal one: ¿Cómo estás? ¡Qué bien! Spanish uses fewer capital letters than English: days, months, languages and nationalities are written in lower case (lunes, enero, español, mexicano). Names, place names and the first word of a sentence are capitalized.

sections.title: Nouns, gender, articles and plurals
sections.summary: Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine, and the articles, adjectives and pronouns around it must agree. This chapter gives you the gender patterns, the four forms of 'the', the plural rules and the two contractions al and del.

rules.title: Every noun has a gender
rules.body: Spanish nouns are either masculine or feminine, even for objects. Most nouns ending in -o are masculine (el libro, el coche) and most ending in -a are feminine (la casa, la mesa). Nouns ending in -e or a consonant can be either and must be learned with their article: el coche, la noche, el papel, la ciudad.

rules.title: Definite and indefinite articles
rules.body: 'The' has four forms: el (masculine singular), la (feminine singular), los (masculine plural), las (feminine plural). 'A / an' and 'some' have four forms too: un, una, unos, unas. The article always agrees with the noun in gender and number.

rules.title: Useful endings and exceptions
rules.body: Nouns ending in -ción, -sión, -dad, -tad, -tud and -umbre are feminine: la nación, la televisión, la ciudad, la libertad, la costumbre. Nouns of Greek origin ending in -ma are masculine: el problema, el sistema, el programa, el clima. Other common exceptions: el día, el mapa, el planeta are masculine; la mano, la foto (fotografía), la moto (motocicleta), la radio are feminine.

rules.title: el agua: feminine nouns with stressed a-
rules.body: A feminine singular noun that begins with a stressed a- or ha- takes el and un instead of la and una, just to avoid two a sounds in a row: el agua, el águila, el hambre, un alma. The noun is still feminine, so adjectives stay feminine (el agua fría) and the plural uses las (las aguas, las águilas).

rules.title: Forming the plural
rules.body: Add -s to a noun ending in a vowel (casa, casas; estudiante, estudiantes) and -es to one ending in a consonant (ciudad, ciudades; papel, papeles). A final -z changes to -ces: lápiz, lápices; vez, veces. Nouns ending in unstressed -s do not change: el lunes, los lunes; la crisis, las crisis. Watch the written accent: canción, canciones (accent lost); examen, exámenes (accent gained).

rules.title: The contractions al and del
rules.body: When a or de is followed by el, they always join: a + el = al, de + el = del. Voy al mercado (I'm going to the market); el libro del profesor (the teacher's book). There is no contraction with la, los or las, nor with the pronoun él: Voy a la playa; Hablo de él.

rules.title: Nouns for people
rules.body: Nouns for people usually change -o to -a for a woman (el chico, la chica; el abogado, la abogada) and add -a to -or (el profesor, la profesora). Nouns ending in -ista or -e often have one form for both genders, and only the article changes: el / la periodista, el / la estudiante. A mixed group uses the masculine plural: los padres (the parents), los hermanos (the brothers and sisters).

rules.title: When to use the article
rules.body: Spanish uses the definite article more than English: with nouns used in a general sense (Me gusta el café: I like coffee), with days of the week to mean 'on' (el lunes: on Monday), with times (a las dos), and with titles when talking about someone (el señor García). No article is used after ser with an unmodified profession or nationality: Soy médico. Es española.

sections.title: Ser vs estar and the present tense
sections.summary: Spanish has two verbs for 'to be' and three regular verb patterns in the present tense. This chapter covers the endings, the ser/estar distinction, stem-changing verbs and the 'go' verbs you will use constantly.

rules.title: Subject pronouns and regular -ar verbs
rules.body: The subject pronouns are yo, tú, él/ella/usted, nosotros/as, vosotros/as, ellos/ellas/ustedes. Regular -ar verbs drop -ar and add -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an: hablar gives hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan. The ending shows the subject, so the pronoun is usually left out.

rules.title: Regular -er and -ir verbs
rules.body: -er verbs take -o, -es, -e, -emos, -éis, -en: comer gives como, comes, come, comemos, coméis, comen. -ir verbs are the same except for nosotros and vosotros: vivir gives vivo, vives, vive, vivimos, vivís, viven. The only difference between the two groups is -emos/-éis versus -imos/-ís.

rules.title: ser: what something is
rules.body: ser is irregular: soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son. Use it for identity and definitions, origin and nationality, profession, inherent characteristics, possession, time and dates: Soy Ana. Es de Chile. Somos estudiantes. Mi casa es pequeña. Es la una. Hoy es martes.

rules.title: estar: where and how something is
rules.body: estar is also irregular: estoy, estás, está, estamos, estáis, están. Use it for location, temporary states and conditions, feelings and health, and for the progressive (estar + -ando/-iendo): Madrid está en España. Estoy cansado. La sopa está fría. Estamos comiendo.

rules.title: Adjectives that change meaning with ser / estar
rules.body: Some adjectives mean different things depending on the verb. ser aburrido = boring, estar aburrido = bored; ser listo = clever, estar listo = ready; ser rico = rich, estar rico = tasty; ser malo = bad, estar malo = ill. In general ser describes what something is like by nature and estar describes its state right now.

rules.title: Stem-changing verbs
rules.body: Many verbs change the vowel of the stem in every form except nosotros and vosotros (the 'boot' pattern). e becomes ie: querer, quiero, quieres, quiere, queremos, queréis, quieren; also pensar, empezar, entender, preferir. o becomes ue: poder, puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, podéis, pueden; also dormir, volver, costar; jugar changes u to ue. e becomes i in some -ir verbs: pedir, pido, pides, pide, pedimos, pedís, piden; also servir, repetir.

rules.title: The 'go' verbs and other irregular yo forms
rules.body: Several common verbs are regular except for a yo form ending in -go: tener (tengo), hacer (hago), poner (pongo), salir (salgo), venir (vengo), decir (digo), traer (traigo). tener, venir and decir also change their stem: tienes, vienes, dices. A few other verbs have irregular yo forms: ir (voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van), ver (veo), saber (sé), dar (doy), conocer (conozco).

rules.title: Expressions with tener
rules.body: Spanish uses tener (to have) where English uses 'to be' for many states: tener hambre (to be hungry), tener sed (thirsty), tener frío (cold), tener calor (hot), tener sueño (sleepy), tener miedo (afraid), tener razón (to be right), tener prisa (in a hurry). Age also uses tener: Tengo veinte años. tener que + infinitive means 'to have to'.

sections.title: Adjectives, possessives and agreement
sections.summary: Adjectives in Spanish agree with their noun and usually follow it, a few shorten before it, and possessives agree with the thing owned rather than the owner. This chapter also covers comparison with más, menos and tan.

rules.title: Adjective agreement
rules.body: An adjective agrees with its noun in gender and number. Adjectives ending in -o have four forms: alto, alta, altos, altas. Adjectives ending in -e or a consonant have only two forms, singular and plural: grande, grandes; azul, azules; fácil, fáciles. Adjectives of nationality ending in a consonant do add -a for the feminine: español, española; alemán, alemana.

examples.target: un chico alto, una chica alta
examples.en: a tall boy, a tall girl

rules.title: Position: usually after the noun
rules.body: Descriptive adjectives normally follow the noun: un coche rojo, una ciudad bonita. Quantity words and demonstratives come before: muchos libros, este libro, tres amigos. A few adjectives change meaning with position: un viejo amigo (a long-time friend) vs un amigo viejo (an elderly friend); un gran hombre (a great man) vs un hombre grande (a big man); una nueva casa (a new, different house) vs una casa nueva (a brand-new house).

rules.title: Shortened adjectives: buen, gran, primer
rules.body: Before a masculine singular noun, bueno, malo, primero, tercero, alguno and ninguno drop the final -o: un buen día, mal tiempo, el primer piso, el tercer año, algún problema, ningún libro (algún and ningún gain an accent). grande becomes gran before any singular noun, masculine or feminine: un gran hombre, una gran ciudad. The full forms are used after the noun or in the feminine and plural: una buena idea, un hombre bueno.

rules.title: Possessive adjectives: mi, tu, su...
rules.body: The short possessives go before the noun: mi, tu, su, nuestro, vuestro, su. They agree in number with the thing owned, not with the owner: mi libro, mis libros; su casa, sus casas. nuestro and vuestro also agree in gender: nuestra casa, nuestros amigos. su / sus can mean his, her, its, their or your (usted), so when it is unclear Spanish adds de él, de ella, de usted: la casa de ella.

rules.title: Stressed possessives: mío, tuyo, suyo
rules.body: The long forms mío, tuyo, suyo, nuestro, vuestro, suyo come after the noun or stand alone, and agree with it in gender and number: un amigo mío (a friend of mine), Es mía (It's mine), el tuyo (yours). With an article they work as pronouns: Mi casa es grande, la tuya es pequeña.

examples.target: Tu coche es nuevo; el mío es viejo.
examples.en: Your car is new; mine is old.

rules.title: Comparison: más que, menos que, tan como
rules.body: More than is más + adjective + que, less than is menos + adjective + que, and as ... as is tan + adjective + como: Ana es más alta que Luis. El tren es menos caro que el avión. Pedro es tan listo como tú. Four adjectives have irregular comparatives: bueno, mejor (better); malo, peor (worse); grande, mayor (older / greater); pequeño, menor (younger / lesser). With numbers use más de: más de diez euros.

examples.en: My house is bigger than yours.

examples.target: Es tan simpático como su hermano.
examples.en: He is as nice as his brother.

examples.target: Este libro es mejor que ese.
examples.en: This book is better than that one.
I am older than my cousin.

rules.title: Superlatives
rules.body: The superlative is article + noun + más / menos + adjective, and 'in' is de: la chica más alta de la clase, el restaurante menos caro de la ciudad; with irregulars: el mejor equipo, mi hermano mayor. The ending -ísimo adds 'extremely': altísimo, facilísimo, muchísimo. Do not combine muy with -ísimo.

examples.target: Es el mejor restaurante de Madrid.
examples.en: It is the best restaurant in Madrid.

examples.target: la ciudad más grande del país
examples.en: the biggest city in the country

rules.title: Demonstratives: este, ese, aquel
rules.body: Spanish has three distances: este (this, near me), ese (that, near you), aquel (that over there). They agree with the noun: este libro, esta casa, estos libros, estas casas; ese, esa, esos, esas; aquel, aquella, aquellos, aquellas. Used alone they are pronouns: Quiero este. The neuter forms esto, eso, aquello refer to an idea or an unknown thing: ¿Qué es esto?

rules.title: mucho, poco, todo and muy
rules.body: mucho, poco, todo, otro and demasiado are adjectives and agree with the noun: mucha gente, pocos amigos, todas las chicas, otra vez. muy is an adverb and never changes: muy alta, muy altos. Before an adjective or adverb use muy; before a noun use mucho/a/os/as; after a verb use the invariable mucho: Trabaja mucho.

examples.en: She is very intelligent and works a lot.

sections.title: Pronouns: subject, object and reflexive
sections.summary: Spanish drops subject pronouns, puts object pronouns before the verb and uses reflexive pronouns for daily routines. This chapter also explains gustar, which turns the English sentence around.

rules.title: Dropping the subject pronoun
rules.body: Because the verb ending shows the subject, pronouns like yo, tú and nosotros are usually left out: Hablo inglés, not Yo hablo inglés. They are used for emphasis or contrast (Yo trabajo, pero él no) and to avoid confusion with él/ella/usted, which share the same verb form. usted (formal you) and ustedes take the third-person verb forms. In Spain vosotros is the informal plural; in Latin America ustedes is used for everyone.

examples.target: Yo quiero té, pero ella quiere café.
examples.en: I want tea, but she wants coffee.

rules.title: Direct object pronouns
rules.body: The direct object pronouns are me, te, lo, la, nos, os, los, las. lo / los replace masculine nouns and la / las feminine ones, for people and things: ¿Tienes el libro? Lo tengo. Veo a María. La veo. The pronoun goes immediately before the conjugated verb, after no: No lo veo. In Spain le is often used instead of lo for a male person (leísmo), but lo is correct everywhere.

rules.title: Indirect object pronouns and se
rules.body: The indirect object pronouns ('to / for' someone) are me, te, le, nos, os, les: Le doy el libro (I give him the book). Spanish often keeps the pronoun even when the person is named: Le escribo a mi madre. When le or les meets lo, la, los or las, it becomes se: Se lo doy (I give it to him). The order is always indirect before direct: Te lo digo. Me la compra.

examples.target: Le doy el libro a Juan.
examples.en: I give the book to Juan.
I give it to him / her / them.

rules.title: Where the pronoun goes
rules.body: Before a conjugated verb: Lo compro. With an infinitive or gerund, the pronoun can attach to the end or go before the conjugated verb: Voy a comprarlo / Lo voy a comprar; Estoy leyéndolo / Lo estoy leyendo. With affirmative commands the pronoun must attach: Dímelo (tell it to me), Cómpralo. An accent is often added to keep the original stress when pronouns are attached.

rules.title: Reflexive verbs
rules.body: A reflexive verb has the pronouns me, te, se, nos, os, se and describes something you do to yourself or a change of state: lavarse, me lavo (I wash myself); levantarse, me levanto (I get up); acostarse, me acuesto; vestirse, me visto; llamarse, me llamo (my name is). Many daily-routine verbs are reflexive. In the plural the same forms can be reciprocal: Nos vemos mañana (we'll see each other tomorrow).

rules.title: gustar: 'to be pleasing'
rules.body: gustar works backwards from English 'like': the thing liked is the subject and the person is an indirect object. Me gusta el café (coffee is pleasing to me = I like coffee); Me gustan los perros (plural subject, plural verb). Use a + person for emphasis or clarity: A Juan le gusta bailar. A mí me gusta. Verbs that work the same way: encantar (to love), interesar, importar, doler (to hurt), faltar, parecer, molestar.

rules.title: Pronouns after prepositions
rules.body: After a preposition (para, de, sin, a, en...) Spanish uses mí, ti, él, ella, usted, nosotros, vosotros, ellos, ellas, ustedes: para mí, sin ti, de ella. con has two special forms: conmigo (with me) and contigo (with you). After entre and según the subject forms are used: entre tú y yo.

exercises.explain: libro is masculine singular, so the direct object pronoun is lo.

exercises.q: Veo a María todos los días. ___ veo todos los días.
exercises.explain: María is a feminine direct object, so la.

exercises.q: Subject pronouns such as 'yo' are usually left out in Spanish.
exercises.explain: The verb ending already shows the subject; yo is added only for emphasis or contrast.
los perros is the subject of gustar, so the verb is plural.
llamarse is reflexive: me llamo, te llamas, se llama.

exercises.answer: Me levanto a las siete.
exercises.en: I get up at seven.

exercises.explain: gustar takes an indirect object pronoun: le for ella.
Indirect (te) comes before direct (lo), and libro is masculine.

exercises.q: 'Le lo doy' is correct Spanish for 'I give it to him'.
exercises.explain: le becomes se before lo: Se lo doy.

exercises.q: Compro flores para mi madre. ___ compro flores a mi madre.
exercises.explain: mi madre is the indirect object, so le is used, even with 'a mi madre' present.

exercises.q: Replace 'el pan' with a pronoun in 'Voy a comprar el pan.'
exercises.explain: With an infinitive the pronoun attaches to its end (or goes before voy: Lo voy a comprar).
acostarse is reflexive and stem-changing: se acuestan.

exercises.answer: A mí me encanta la música.
exercises.en: I love music.

exercises.explain: After a preposition the form is mí with an accent.
con + mí becomes the special form conmigo; 'with you' is contigo.
'with me' is the single word conmigo, never 'con mí'.
doler works like gustar and takes an indirect object pronoun.
las películas is a plural subject, so interesan.

exercises.answer: Se lo digo a mi hermano.
exercises.en: I tell it to my brother.

exercises.explain: Literally 'you are pleasing to me'; the person liked is the subject, so the verb is gustas.

exercises.q: ¿Conoces a mis primos? No, no ___ conozco.
exercises.explain: primos is masculine plural, so the direct object pronoun is los.
da (give) + me (to me) + lo (it): the pronouns attach to the affirmative command.
lavarse is reflexive: se lava las manos (she washes her hands).

exercises.q: In Spain 'vosotros' is the informal plural 'you', while Latin America uses 'ustedes' for everyone.
exercises.explain: vosotros forms are used in Spain only; Latin America uses ustedes with third-person plural verbs.

exercises.answer: ¿Te gusta bailar conmigo?
exercises.en: Do you like dancing with me?

exercises.q: Mis padres ___ escriben a mí cada semana.
exercises.explain: The indirect object pronoun me is required; 'a mí' only adds emphasis.
usted takes the third-person singular verb form, like él or ella.

sections.title: Preterite vs imperfect
sections.summary: Spanish has two simple past tenses: the preterite for completed events and the imperfect for background, habits and descriptions. This chapter gives both sets of forms, the key irregulars and the logic for choosing between them.

rules.title: Regular preterite forms
rules.body: The preterite of -ar verbs: hablé, hablaste, habló, hablamos, hablasteis, hablaron. -er and -ir verbs share one set: comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comisteis, comieron; viví, viviste, vivió, vivimos, vivisteis, vivieron. Note the accents on the yo and él forms. The nosotros form of -ar and -ir verbs is identical to the present (hablamos, vivimos); context tells you which is meant.

examples.en: Yesterday I spoke to my mother.

examples.target: Ella vivió en Chile dos años.
examples.en: She lived in Chile for two years.

rules.title: Spelling changes in the preterite
rules.body: To keep the sound of the stem, the yo form changes spelling: -car becomes -qué (buscar, busqué), -gar becomes -gué (llegar, llegué; jugar, jugué), -zar becomes -cé (empezar, empecé). Verbs whose stem ends in a vowel write y instead of i in the él and ellos forms: leer, leyó, leyeron; oír, oyó, oyeron; creer, creyó.

examples.target: Leyó el libro en un día.
examples.en: He read the book in one day.

rules.title: Irregular preterites
rules.body: ser and ir share the same preterite: fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron. A group of verbs has an irregular stem plus the endings -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -isteis, -ieron, with no accents: tener, tuve; estar, estuve; hacer, hice (él: hizo); poder, pude; poner, puse; querer, quise; venir, vine; saber, supe. decir (dije) and traer (traje) take -eron in the ellos form: dijeron, trajeron. dar and ver are short: di, diste, dio; vi, viste, vio.

examples.en: I went to the cinema last night.

rules.title: Stem-changing -ir verbs in the preterite
rules.body: Only -ir verbs change their stem in the preterite, and only in the él and ellos forms: e becomes i and o becomes u. pedir: pidió, pidieron; servir: sirvió, sirvieron; preferir: prefirió, prefirieron; dormir: durmió, durmieron; morir: murió, murieron. -ar and -er verbs such as pensar, volver and querer have no stem change in the preterite (pensó, volvió).

rules.title: Imperfect forms
rules.body: The imperfect is very regular. -ar verbs: hablaba, hablabas, hablaba, hablábamos, hablabais, hablaban. -er and -ir verbs: comía, comías, comía, comíamos, comíais, comían; vivía, vivías... Only three verbs are irregular: ser (era, eras, era, éramos, erais, eran), ir (iba, ibas, iba, íbamos, ibais, iban) and ver (veía, veías, veía, veíamos, veíais, veían).

examples.target: Hablaba con mi abuela cada semana.
examples.en: I used to talk to my grandmother every week.
We lived in a small village.

examples.target: Íbamos a la playa en verano.
examples.en: We used to go to the beach in summer.

rules.title: When to use the preterite
rules.body: The preterite reports a completed action or event seen as a whole, often with a specific time or a clear beginning and end: Ayer comí pescado. Vivió en París tres años. It moves a story forward, one event after another: Me levanté, desayuné y salí. Typical markers: ayer, anoche, la semana pasada, el año pasado, en 2010, de repente, una vez.

examples.en: Last night we watched a film.
I got up, had breakfast and left.
He studied in Salamanca for two years.

rules.title: When to use the imperfect
rules.body: The imperfect describes the past without focusing on its end: habits and repeated actions (used to, would), descriptions of people, places and weather, age, time and feelings, and actions in progress. Typical markers: siempre, todos los días, a menudo, de niño, mientras, antes. Hacía frío. Tenía diez años. Eran las ocho. Estaba cansada.

examples.target: De niño jugaba al fútbol todos los días.
examples.en: As a child I played football every day.

examples.target: Hacía sol y la gente paseaba.
examples.en: It was sunny and people were strolling.

rules.title: Using both tenses together
rules.body: In a story, the imperfect sets the scene and the preterite tells what happened. An action in progress (imperfect) is often interrupted by a sudden event (preterite), typically with cuando or mientras: Dormía cuando sonó el teléfono. Mientras cenábamos, llegó Juan. Two ongoing actions at the same time both take the imperfect: Yo leía mientras ella cocinaba.

examples.en: I was sleeping when the phone rang.
While we were having dinner, Juan arrived.

examples.target: Llovía, así que nos quedamos en casa.
examples.en: It was raining, so we stayed at home.

rules.title: Verbs that change meaning
rules.body: A few verbs shift meaning between the two tenses. saber: sabía (knew) but supe (found out). conocer: conocía (knew a person or place) but conocí (met for the first time). querer: quería (wanted) but quise (tried to) and no quise (refused). poder: podía (was able, in general) but pude (managed to) and no pude (failed to). tener: tenía (had) but tuve (got, received).

examples.en: I found out the truth yesterday.

exercises.explain: The yo preterite of an -ar verb is -é, with an accent.
-er verbs take -imos in the nosotros preterite.

exercises.q: The preterite is used for actions seen as completed in the past.
exercises.explain: Ayer comí pescado: a finished event with a clear time.

exercises.q: Cuando era niño, ___ al fútbol todos los días. (jugar)
exercises.explain: A repeated, habitual action in the past takes the imperfect.

exercises.q: Mi abuela ___ (vivir, imperfect) en un pueblo pequeño.
exercises.explain: -ir verbs take -ía in the imperfect: vivía.

exercises.answer: Ayer fui al cine con mis amigos.
exercises.en: Yesterday I went to the cinema with my friends.

exercises.q: Ellos ___ a Madrid el año pasado. (ir)
exercises.explain: A single completed trip with a specific time uses the preterite: fueron.

exercises.q: 'fui' can mean both 'I went' and 'I was'.
exercises.explain: ser and ir share the same preterite forms.
tener has the irregular preterite stem tuv-: tuve, no accent.
-gar verbs write -gué in the yo preterite to keep the hard g sound.
Telling the time in the past uses the imperfect: eran las ocho.

exercises.q: The imperfect has only three irregular verbs: ser, ir and ver.
exercises.explain: era, iba and veía are the only irregular imperfects.

exercises.q: Mientras yo ___, mi hermano ___ por teléfono. (an ongoing action interrupted by a single event)
exercises.explain: The action in progress takes the imperfect and the interrupting event takes the preterite.

exercises.answer: Hacía sol y los niños jugaban en la calle.
exercises.en: It was sunny and the children were playing in the street.

exercises.explain: hacer has the irregular preterite hice, hiciste, hizo; the c becomes z before o.
-ir stem-changing verbs change e to i in the él form of the preterite.

exercises.q: What does 'Conocí a Luis en 2010' mean?
options: I used to know Luis in 2010
exercises.explain: In the preterite conocer means 'to meet for the first time'.

exercises.q: 'Sabía la respuesta' means 'I found out the answer'.
exercises.explain: sabía means 'I knew'; 'I found out' is supe.
A description of what people were like uses the imperfect of ser: eran.

exercises.q: Nosotros ___ a la playa cada verano. (ir)
exercises.explain: 'Every summer' marks a habit, so the imperfect íbamos.

exercises.answer: De repente sonó el teléfono.
exercises.en: Suddenly the phone rang.

exercises.q: What is the 'ellos' preterite form of 'decir'?
exercises.explain: Stems ending in j take -eron, not -ieron: dijeron, trajeron.

exercises.q: Yo ___ (empezar, preterite) a estudiar a las seis.
exercises.explain: -zar verbs change z to c before é: empecé.

exercises.q: In 'Dormía cuando llegaste', 'dormía' describes an action that was in progress.
exercises.explain: The imperfect gives the background action; the preterite llegaste is the event that interrupts it.
no quiso in the preterite means refused; no quería would be 'didn't want to'.

exercises.answer: Cuando era pequeña, tenía un perro.
exercises.en: When I was little, I had a dog.

exercises.explain: dormir changes o to u in the ellos preterite: durmieron.

exercises.q: Yo ___ esa película la semana pasada. (ver)
exercises.explain: ver has the short preterite vi, written without an accent.

sections.title: The future, conditional and perfect tenses
sections.summary: Spanish talks about the future with ir a or with one set of endings added to the infinitive, uses the conditional for 'would', and builds perfect tenses with haber plus a past participle. This chapter gives the forms, the shared irregular stems and the main uses.

rules.title: ir a + infinitive: the near future
rules.body: The most common way to talk about the future in speech is a present form of ir + a + infinitive: Voy a comer. ¿Vas a venir? Vamos a estudiar. It corresponds to English 'going to'. Vamos a + infinitive can also mean 'let's': ¡Vamos a bailar!

examples.en: I am going to study tonight.
Are you going to come to the party?
We are going to eat / Let's eat.

rules.title: The simple future
rules.body: The future is formed by adding -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án to the whole infinitive, for all three verb groups: hablaré, hablarás, hablará, hablaremos, hablaréis, hablarán; comeré; viviré. It is used for predictions, promises and more distant plans: Mañana lloverá. Te llamaré. Every form except nosotros carries an accent.

examples.en: I will call you this afternoon.

rules.title: Irregular future stems
rules.body: Twelve common verbs use a shortened stem with the regular future endings: tener, tendr- (tendré); poner, pondr-; salir, saldr-; venir, vendr-; valer, valdr-; poder, podr-; saber, sabr-; haber, habr- (habrá = there will be); querer, querr-; hacer, har- (haré); decir, dir- (diré). The same stems are used for the conditional.

examples.en: What will you do on Saturday?
I will tell you the truth.

rules.title: The future of probability
rules.body: Spanish uses the future tense to guess or wonder about the present: ¿Qué hora será? (I wonder what time it is.) Serán las tres. (It must be about three.) ¿Dónde estará Juan? Estará en casa. (He is probably at home.) The conditional does the same for the past: Serían las tres cuando llegó. (It must have been about three when he arrived.)

examples.en: I wonder what time it is.

rules.title: The conditional
rules.body: The conditional adds -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían to the infinitive (or to the irregular future stem): hablaría, comería, viviría, tendría, haría, diría. It translates 'would': Me gustaría viajar. It softens requests and advice (¿Podrías ayudarme? Deberías descansar), reports the future from the past (Dijo que vendría), and expresses hypothetical results (Con más dinero compraría una casa).

examples.en: He said he would come tomorrow.

rules.title: The present perfect: he hablado
rules.body: The present perfect is haber (he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han) + past participle: -ar verbs form the participle in -ado (hablado) and -er/-ir verbs in -ido (comido, vivido). It is used for recent events and for life experience: He comido ya. ¿Has estado en México? In Spain it also covers today and this week (Hoy he trabajado mucho), where Latin America prefers the preterite (Hoy trabajé mucho). Common markers: ya, todavía no, nunca, alguna vez, hoy, esta semana.

examples.en: Have you ever been to Mexico?

rules.title: Irregular past participles
rules.body: A few participles must be learned: hacer, hecho; decir, dicho; ver, visto; poner, puesto; escribir, escrito; abrir, abierto; romper, roto; volver, vuelto; morir, muerto; cubrir, cubierto; resolver, resuelto. Compounds follow the same pattern: describir, descrito; devolver, devuelto. Participles with -aído/-eído/-oído carry an accent: traído, leído, oído.

examples.en: They have opened a new shop.

rules.title: Pluperfect, future perfect and conditional perfect
rules.body: All the perfect tenses use a form of haber plus the participle. Pluperfect (had done): había, habías, había, habíamos, habíais, habían + participle: Cuando llegué, ya habían salido. Future perfect (will have done): habré, habrás, habrá... : Para junio habré terminado. Conditional perfect (would have done): habría, habrías, habría... : Yo habría ido, pero estaba enfermo.

examples.en: By June I will have finished.

rules.title: Rules for haber + participle
rules.body: After haber the participle never changes: Ella ha vuelto, Ellas han vuelto. Nothing can go between haber and the participle: object and reflexive pronouns go before haber (Lo he visto. Me he levantado. No lo he hecho), and ya or nunca go before haber or after the participle, never between them. haber is only an auxiliary here; 'to have' in the sense of possession is tener.

exercises.explain: ir a + infinitive uses the present of ir: voy a estudiar.

exercises.q: Nosotros ___ (hablar, future) con el jefe mañana.
exercises.explain: The future adds -emos to the infinitive: hablaremos.

exercises.q: The simple future endings are the same for -ar, -er and -ir verbs.
exercises.explain: -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án are added to any infinitive.

exercises.q: Yo ___ en casa esta noche. (comer, future)
exercises.explain: The yo future form is infinitive + -é.
The present perfect uses he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han.

exercises.answer: Voy a visitar a mi abuela.
exercises.en: I am going to visit my grandmother.

exercises.q: What is the past participle of 'hacer'?
exercises.explain: hacer has the irregular participle hecho.
he (I have) + hecho (done).
salir uses the irregular stem saldr-: saldrán.

exercises.q: Me ___ un café, por favor. (gustar, conditional)
exercises.explain: The conditional of gustar makes a polite request: me gustaría.
poder uses the stem podr- plus -ías: podrías, a polite 'could you'.

exercises.answer: Hemos comido en un restaurante italiano.
exercises.en: We have eaten in an Italian restaurant.

options: a guess or wondering about the present
exercises.explain: The future of probability: 'I wonder what time it is'.

exercises.q: In 'Lo he visto', the pronoun could also go between 'he' and 'visto'.
exercises.explain: Nothing can separate haber from the participle; pronouns go before haber.
The pluperfect is había/habían + participle for an action completed before another past action.
tener uses the irregular stem tendr- with the yo ending -é.
habría + participle is the conditional perfect: would have.
volver has the irregular participle vuelto; the auxiliary for ella is ha.

exercises.answer: Me gustaría viajar a Chile.
exercises.en: I would like to travel to Chile.

exercises.q: 'Vamos a comer' can mean both 'we are going to eat' and 'let's eat'.
exercises.explain: vamos a + infinitive doubles as a suggestion.
venir uses the stem vendr- and the vosotros ending -éis.
ver has the irregular participle visto.

exercises.q: Complete with the present perfect: Hoy ___ mucho. (trabajar, yo)
exercises.explain: he + the -ado participle; the gerund trabajando is not used with haber.

exercises.q: The participle after 'haber' agrees with the subject, so 'Ella ha vuelta' is correct.
exercises.explain: After haber the participle never changes: Ella ha vuelto.

exercises.answer: Nunca he estado en Perú.
exercises.en: I have never been to Peru.

exercises.q: Someone without a watch says 'Serán las tres'. What do they mean?
options: It must be about three o'clock
It will be three o'clock tomorrow
exercises.explain: The future tense expresses a guess about the present.
The conditional reports a future seen from the past: he said he would come.

exercises.q: Which is the correct conditional 'yo' form of 'hacer'?
exercises.explain: hacer uses the shortened stem har- in both the future and the conditional.

sections.title: The subjunctive, part 1
sections.summary: The present subjunctive appears after que whenever the main clause expresses a wish, an emotion, a doubt or a judgement rather than a fact. This chapter gives the forms and the most common triggers.

rules.title: What the subjunctive is for
rules.body: The indicative states facts: Sé que viene (I know he is coming). The subjunctive is used in a clause introduced by que when the main verb expresses a wish, request, emotion, doubt or judgement about that clause: Quiero que venga (I want him to come). English often uses an infinitive or 'that ... should'; Spanish needs que + subjunctive whenever the two clauses have different subjects.

rules.title: Regular present subjunctive forms
rules.body: Start from the yo form of the present indicative, drop the -o and add the 'opposite' endings. -ar verbs take -e, -es, -e, -emos, -éis, -en: hable, hables, hable, hablemos, habléis, hablen. -er and -ir verbs take -a, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an: coma, comas...; viva, vivas... Because you start from the yo form, irregular yo forms carry over: tener, tenga; hacer, haga; poner, ponga; salir, salga; venir, venga; decir, diga; conocer, conozca; ver, vea.

examples.en: I want you to talk to her.
It is important that you eat well.
I don't think it is cold.

rules.title: Stem and spelling changes
rules.body: Stem-changing verbs keep their change in the subjunctive: querer, quiera, quieras, quiera, queramos, queráis, quieran; poder, pueda... In -ir verbs the nosotros and vosotros forms also change: dormir, durmamos, durmáis; pedir, pidamos, pidáis; sentir, sintamos. Spelling adjusts to keep the sound: buscar, busque; llegar, llegue; empezar, empiece; escoger, escoja.

examples.en: She wants us to ask for the bill.
It is necessary that you arrive early.

rules.title: Six irregular verbs
rules.body: Six verbs have irregular subjunctive stems that must be memorised: ser, sea, seas, sea, seamos, seáis, sean; estar, esté, estés, esté, estemos, estéis, estén; ir, vaya, vayas, vaya, vayamos, vayáis, vayan; haber, haya; saber, sepa, sepas...; dar, dé, des, dé, demos, deis, den. Note the accents on esté and dé.

examples.en: I want you to be happy.
It is better that we go now.

rules.title: Wishes and influence: querer que, pedir que
rules.body: Verbs of wanting, hoping, asking and advising trigger the subjunctive when the subject changes: querer que, esperar que, necesitar que, pedir que, decir que (telling someone to), recomendar que, aconsejar que, prohibir que, preferir que. If the subject is the same, use the infinitive instead: Quiero comer (I want to eat) but Quiero que comas (I want you to eat).

examples.target: Quiero que vengas a mi fiesta.
examples.en: I want you to come to my party.
I recommend that you sleep more.

rules.title: Emotion: me alegro de que, es una pena que
rules.body: Expressions of feeling about something also take the subjunctive: alegrarse de que, me gusta que, me molesta que, sentir que (to be sorry that), tener miedo de que, es una pena / lástima que, es triste que, es sorprendente que. The feeling is in the main clause; the event it reacts to goes into the subjunctive.

examples.target: Me alegro de que estés aquí.
examples.en: I am glad you are here.

examples.target: Es una pena que no puedas venir.
examples.en: It is a pity you can't come.
I am sorry you feel bad.

rules.title: Doubt and denial: no creo que, dudar que
rules.body: Doubt, denial and uncertainty trigger the subjunctive: dudar que, no creer que, no pensar que, no es verdad que, no es cierto que, es posible que, es probable que, puede que. But creer que, pensar que, es verdad que, es evidente que and es cierto que state what the speaker holds to be true and take the indicative: Creo que tiene razón, No creo que tenga razón.

examples.en: I don't think he is right.
It is possible that it will rain.

rules.title: ojalá, quizás and que + subjunctive
rules.body: ojalá (que) means 'I hope' or 'if only' and always takes the subjunctive: Ojalá llueva. Ojalá que apruebes. quizás and tal vez (perhaps) take the subjunctive when the speaker is doubtful: Quizás venga mañana. A clause starting with que + subjunctive expresses a wish for someone: ¡Que tengas buen viaje! ¡Que te mejores! ¡Que aproveche!

rules.title: Impersonal expressions: es importante que
rules.body: Impersonal judgements with ser + adjective + que take the subjunctive: es importante que, es necesario que, es mejor que, es bueno / malo que, es normal que, es raro que, es urgente que, es difícil que. Without a specific subject the infinitive is used: Es importante estudiar. Expressions of certainty are the exception and take the indicative: es verdad que, es evidente que, es obvio que, está claro que.

examples.en: It is important that you study.
It is better that you go now.
It is true that it is expensive.

exercises.q: Quiero que tú ___ a la fiesta. (venir)
exercises.explain: querer que with a different subject takes the subjunctive: vengas.
es importante que triggers the subjunctive; -ar verbs take -emos.

exercises.q: After 'querer que' with a change of subject, the verb goes in the subjunctive.
exercises.explain: Quiero que vengas: I want you to come.
ojalá always takes the subjunctive: llueva.
esperar que triggers the subjunctive; estar gives esté with an accent.

exercises.answer: Quiero que vengas a mi fiesta.
exercises.en: I want you to come to my party.

exercises.explain: creer que in the affirmative states a belief and takes the indicative.

exercises.q: 'Es verdad que' is followed by the subjunctive.
exercises.explain: Expressions of certainty take the indicative: Es verdad que es caro.
no creer que expresses doubt and takes the subjunctive: tengas.
When the subject does not change, the infinitive is used, not que + subjunctive.
After querer que the -er verb takes the subjunctive ending -as.

exercises.answer: Es necesario que hables con ella.
exercises.en: It is necessary that you talk to her.

exercises.explain: alegrarse de que expresses emotion and takes the subjunctive.

exercises.q: After 'ojalá' you always use the subjunctive.
exercises.explain: ojalá expresses a wish and never takes the indicative.

exercises.q: Es posible que nosotros ___ al cine. (ir)
exercises.explain: es posible que expresses uncertainty; ir has the irregular subjunctive vaya, vayamos.
dudar que takes the subjunctive; saber has the irregular stem sep-.
-car verbs write -que to keep the k sound: busque.

exercises.answer: Ojalá que haga buen tiempo mañana.
exercises.en: I hope the weather is good tomorrow.

exercises.q: 'Es mejor que vas ahora' is correct Spanish.
exercises.explain: es mejor que needs the subjunctive: Es mejor que vayas ahora.
recomendar que triggers the subjunctive; dormir keeps its o to ue change: duermas.

exercises.q: What does '¡Que tengas buen viaje!' mean?
options: Do you have a good trip?
exercises.explain: que + subjunctive expresses a wish for someone.

exercises.q: Es una pena que tú no ___ (poder) venir.
exercises.explain: es una pena que expresses emotion; poder keeps its stem change: puedas.
-ir stem-changing verbs change e to i in the nosotros subjunctive too.

exercises.q: In the present subjunctive, -ar verbs take -e endings and -er/-ir verbs take -a endings.
exercises.explain: The endings are swapped compared with the indicative: hable, coma, viva.

exercises.answer: No creo que sea una buena idea.
exercises.en: I don't think it is a good idea.

exercises.q: Mis padres quieren que yo ___ médico. (ser)
exercises.explain: querer que with a different subject takes the subjunctive; ser gives sea.
-gar verbs write -gue- in the subjunctive to keep the hard g: lleguen.

exercises.q: Which sentence needs the subjunctive in the blank?
exercises.explain: esperar que expresses a hope; the other three state facts or beliefs and take the indicative.

sections.title: Questions, negation and commands
sections.summary: This chapter covers how to ask questions with and without question words, how Spanish stacks negative words, and how to give orders to tú, usted, vosotros and ustedes, including where the pronouns go.

rules.title: Yes / no questions
rules.body: A yes/no question can simply be a statement said with rising intonation: ¿Hablas inglés? The subject, if expressed, often goes after the verb: ¿Vive Juan aquí? You can also add a tag: ¿verdad? or ¿no? (Hablas inglés, ¿no?). Questions are written between ¿ and ?. Answers: Sí, hablo inglés. No, no hablo inglés.

rules.title: Question words
rules.body: The question words all carry an accent: qué (what), quién / quiénes (who), cuál / cuáles (which), dónde (where), adónde (where to), cuándo (when), cómo (how), cuánto / cuánta / cuántos / cuántas (how much, how many), por qué (why). A preposition always goes in front of the question word, never at the end: ¿Con quién vives? ¿De dónde eres? ¿Para qué sirve?

examples.en: Who are you going to the cinema with?
How many sisters do you have?

rules.title: qué vs cuál
rules.body: qué asks for a definition or goes directly before a noun: ¿Qué es esto? ¿Qué libro quieres? cuál asks you to choose from a set and is used before ser when you are not asking for a definition: ¿Cuál es tu nombre? ¿Cuál es la capital de Perú? ¿Cuál prefieres? cuál is not normally used directly before a noun in standard Spanish; use qué instead.

rules.title: Basic negation with no
rules.body: To make a sentence negative, put no directly before the verb, and before any object or reflexive pronouns: No hablo francés. No lo tengo. No me levanto temprano. A negative answer usually repeats no: ¿Tienes coche? No, no tengo coche. Spanish also uses no where English uses 'not': todavía no (not yet), yo no (not me).

examples.en: No, I don't have a car.

rules.title: Negative words and the double negative
rules.body: Negative words: nadie (nobody), nada (nothing), nunca / jamás (never), ninguno / ningún (none, not any), tampoco (neither), ni ... ni (neither ... nor). When a negative word comes after the verb, no is required before the verb: No veo a nadie. No tengo nada. No viene nunca. When it comes before the verb, no is dropped: Nadie viene. Nunca como carne. Several negatives can stack: No le dije nada a nadie.

examples.target: No me gusta el café. Tampoco el té.
examples.en: I don't like coffee. Nor tea.

examples.target: No tengo ni tiempo ni dinero.
examples.en: I have neither time nor money.

rules.title: Affirmative tú commands
rules.body: The affirmative tú command is identical to the él/ella form of the present indicative: habla (speak), come (eat), escribe (write), cierra (close), vuelve (come back). Eight verbs have short irregular commands: decir, di; hacer, haz; ir, ve; poner, pon; salir, sal; ser, sé; tener, ten; venir, ven.

rules.title: Negative tú commands
rules.body: The negative tú command is no + the tú form of the present subjunctive: no hables, no comas, no escribas, no vengas, no hagas, no vayas, no seas. The irregular short forms are only for affirmative commands; the negative always uses the subjunctive.

rules.title: usted, ustedes and vosotros commands
rules.body: usted and ustedes commands use the subjunctive in both the affirmative and the negative: hable / no hable, coma / no coma, venga, vaya, tenga; ustedes: hablen, coman, vengan. The affirmative vosotros command replaces the -r of the infinitive with -d: hablad, comed, venid, id; its negative uses the subjunctive: no habléis, no comáis, no vengáis.

rules.title: Pronouns with commands
rules.body: With affirmative commands, object and reflexive pronouns attach to the end of the verb, and an accent is added to keep the stress: dímelo (tell it to me), cómpralo, levántate, siéntese. With negative commands the pronouns go before the verb as usual: no me lo digas, no lo compres, no te levantes. In the vosotros reflexive command the -d is dropped: sentaos, levantaos.

exercises.explain: dónde asks where; it always carries an accent in a question.
quién asks 'who' and carries an accent.

exercises.q: Written Spanish questions begin with ¿ and end with ?.
exercises.explain: The inverted mark opens the question: ¿Cómo estás?
Before ser, asking for a specific piece of information uses cuál, not qué.
After the verb the negative word nada needs no before the verb.

exercises.answer: ¿De dónde eres tú?
exercises.en: Where are you from?

exercises.explain: nadie after the verb requires no before it, and the personal a before nadie.

exercises.q: 'Nadie viene' needs an extra 'no': 'No nadie viene'.
exercises.explain: When the negative word comes before the verb, no is dropped: Nadie viene.
The affirmative tú command equals the él form of the present: habla.

exercises.q: What is the negative tú command of 'hablar'?
exercises.explain: Negative tú commands use the tú subjunctive: no hables.
venir has the irregular tú command ven.

exercises.answer: No hables tan rápido, por favor.
exercises.en: Don't speak so fast, please.

exercises.q: What is the usted command of 'pasar'?
exercises.explain: usted commands use the usted subjunctive form: pase.

exercises.q: usted commands use the subjunctive forms.
exercises.explain: Hable, coma, venga: the usted command is the usted subjunctive.
cuánto agrees with the noun: cuántas hermanas.

exercises.q: Which question asks for a definition?
exercises.explain: qué asks what something is; cuál asks which one of a set.
tampoco is the negative of también.

exercises.q: No me gusta el café. ___ (neither) me gusta el té.
exercises.explain: tampoco before the verb means 'nor / neither' and needs no extra no.

exercises.answer: ¿Con quién vas al cine?
exercises.en: Who are you going to the cinema with?

exercises.explain: The pronoun attaches to the affirmative command di: dime.

exercises.q: In negative commands the pronouns attach to the verb: 'No dímelo'.
exercises.explain: With negative commands the pronouns go before the verb: No me lo digas.
Negative command: no + pronoun + subjunctive: no te levantes.

exercises.q: What is the ustedes command of 'comer'?
exercises.explain: ustedes commands use the ustedes subjunctive: coman.
ser has the irregular tú command sé, with an accent.

exercises.answer: No conozco a nadie aquí.
exercises.en: I don't know anyone here.

exercises.explain: por qué (two words, accent) asks why; porque (one word) answers because.

exercises.q: Adding '¿verdad?' at the end of a statement turns it into a question, like English 'right?'.
exercises.explain: Tienes hambre, ¿verdad? = You are hungry, right?

exercises.q: What is the affirmative vosotros command of 'escuchar'?
exercises.explain: The vosotros command replaces the -r of the infinitive with -d.

sections.title: Numbers, time, dates and por/para
sections.summary: Counting, telling the time and giving dates are everyday tasks with a few fixed patterns, and por versus para is one of the classic difficulties for English speakers. This chapter puts them together with the common formulas you will hear most.

rules.title: Numbers 0-100
rules.body: 0 cero, 1 uno, 2 dos, 3 tres, 4 cuatro, 5 cinco, 6 seis, 7 siete, 8 ocho, 9 nueve, 10 diez, 11 once, 12 doce, 13 trece, 14 catorce, 15 quince, 16 dieciséis, 17 diecisiete, 18 dieciocho, 19 diecinueve, 20 veinte, 21 veintiuno, 22 veintidós ... 30 treinta. From 31 the tens and units are separate words joined by y: treinta y uno, cuarenta y dos. 40 cuarenta, 50 cincuenta, 60 sesenta, 70 setenta, 80 ochenta, 90 noventa, 100 cien.

rules.title: Hundreds, thousands and agreement
rules.body: 100 is cien before a noun or mil (cien libros, cien mil) and ciento when followed by other numbers (ciento uno). 200-900 end in -cientos and agree with a feminine noun: doscientos hombres, doscientas mujeres; note 500 quinientos, 700 setecientos, 900 novecientos. 1000 mil never takes un and has no plural in counting: dos mil personas. 1,000,000 un millón takes de before a noun: un millón de habitantes. uno shortens to un before a masculine noun and becomes una before a feminine one: veintiún años, treinta y una chicas.

rules.title: Ordinal numbers
rules.body: The ordinals are primero, segundo, tercero, cuarto, quinto, sexto, séptimo, octavo, noveno, décimo. They agree like adjectives (la segunda calle) and primero and tercero shorten to primer and tercer before a masculine singular noun (el primer día, el tercer piso). Above ten, Spanish usually uses cardinal numbers: el siglo veinte, Alfonso trece.

rules.title: Telling the time
rules.body: Ask ¿Qué hora es? Answer with ser: Es la una (one o'clock, singular) but Son las dos, las tres... Minutes past use y: Son las dos y diez; y cuarto (quarter past), y media (half past). Minutes to use menos: Son las tres menos cuarto (2:45). Add de la mañana, de la tarde, de la noche for a.m./p.m. 'At' a time is a la / a las: La clase es a las nueve. Midday and midnight: mediodía, medianoche.

examples.target: Son las ocho menos cuarto de la mañana.
La clase es a las nueve.

rules.title: Days, months and dates
rules.body: Days (lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo) and months (enero, febrero, marzo, abril, mayo, junio, julio, agosto, septiembre, octubre, noviembre, diciembre) are not capitalized. A date is el + cardinal number + de + month + de + year: el doce de octubre de dos mil veinte. Only the first of the month uses an ordinal in Spain, el primero de mayo (Latin America often says el uno de mayo). Ask ¿Qué día es hoy? or ¿A cuántos estamos? Years are read as full numbers: mil novecientos noventa y nueve.

examples.target: Mi cumpleaños es el doce de octubre.

rules.title: por: cause, exchange, movement through, duration
rules.body: por looks back at the reason or the means. Use it for cause or motive (Gracias por el regalo. Lo hago por ti = because of you), exchange and price (Pagué diez euros por el libro), movement through or along (Paseamos por el parque), duration and approximate time (por la mañana, por dos horas), means of communication (por teléfono, por correo), and 'per' (dos veces por semana).

examples.target: Pagué veinte euros por el libro.
examples.en: I paid twenty euros for the book.

rules.title: para: purpose, recipient, destination, deadline
rules.body: para looks forward to a goal. Use it for purpose (Estudio para aprender; una taza para café), the recipient (Este regalo es para ti), destination (Salimos para Madrid), a deadline (Es para mañana), an opinion (Para mí, es caro), and comparison with a standard (Para su edad, habla muy bien). Contrast: Lo hago por ti (because of you) vs Lo hago para ti (for you to have).

examples.target: Estudio español para trabajar en México.
examples.en: I study Spanish in order to work in Mexico.

examples.target: El informe es para el viernes.

examples.en: For me, it is too expensive.

rules.title: Fixed expressions with por and para
rules.body: Many common phrases are fixed: por favor (please), por supuesto (of course), por ejemplo (for example), por fin (at last), por eso (that's why), por lo menos (at least), por ciento (per cent), por cierto (by the way), por la mañana / tarde / noche; para siempre (forever), para nada (not at all), para colmo (to top it all), para que + subjunctive (so that). Learn these as units.

rules.title: hace and desde hace
rules.body: hace + period of time + preterite means 'ago': Fui a Argentina hace tres años. desde hace + period with the present means 'for' (and still true): Vivo aquí desde hace dos años (I have lived here for two years). The same idea can be phrased Hace dos años que vivo aquí. desde alone marks the starting point: desde 2020, desde el lunes.

examples.target: Hace tres años fui a Argentina.
examples.en: Three years ago I went to Argentina.

examples.target: Vivo aquí desde hace dos años.
examples.en: I have lived here for two years.
I have worked here since January.

exercises.explain: quince is 15; cinco is 5 and cincuenta is 50.
21-29 are written as one word: veintidós, with an accent.

exercises.q: 'veintiuno' (21) is written as a single word.
exercises.explain: Numbers 16-29 are single words; from 31 on they are separate: treinta y uno.

exercises.q: How do you say 'It is one o'clock'?
exercises.explain: One o'clock is singular: Es la una; other hours use Son las.
Half past is y media; quarter past is y cuarto.

exercises.answer: Son las cinco menos cuarto.
exercises.en: It is a quarter to five.

exercises.explain: Before a noun, 100 is cien; ciento is used only before other numbers.
Hundreds from 200 to 900 agree in gender with the noun.
The first of the month is el primero in Spain and often el uno in Latin America.
The person who receives something takes para.
Thanks and the reason for them use por.

exercises.answer: Mi cumpleaños es el doce de octubre.
exercises.en: My birthday is October 12.

exercises.explain: para + infinitive expresses purpose: in order to.
por favor is a fixed expression, literally 'as a favour'.

exercises.q: Pagué veinte euros ___ (for, in exchange) el libro.
exercises.explain: Exchange and price take por.

exercises.q: How is the year 2020 said in Spanish?
exercises.explain: Years are read as full numbers; mil has no plural and no y after it.

exercises.q: What time is 'a las ocho de la noche'?
exercises.explain: de la noche marks the evening hours, like p.m.
'At' a time is a la / a las.

exercises.answer: Trabajo por la mañana y estudio por la tarde.
exercises.en: I work in the morning and study in the afternoon.

exercises.q: Dates use ordinal numbers, so 'el cuatro de julio' should be 'el cuarto de julio'.
exercises.explain: Dates use cardinal numbers: el cuatro de julio; only the first may be primero.

exercises.q: How is the number 31 written on its own?
exercises.explain: From 31 on, tens and units are joined by y as separate words.
500 is quinientos, and it agrees with the feminine personas: quinientas.
Movement through or along a place takes por.
y cuarto adds a quarter of an hour to the hour.

exercises.q: What does 'Vivo aquí desde hace dos años' mean?
options: I have lived here for two years
I lived here two years ago
I will live here for two years
I lived here for two years
exercises.explain: desde hace + period with the present tense means 'for' a period that continues now.
millón takes de before a noun: un millón de habitantes.

exercises.answer: Hace tres años fui a Argentina.
exercises.en: Three years ago I went to Argentina.

exercises.explain: 7:45 is a quarter to eight: las ocho menos cuarto.
